candidate.title: Bernardo Kastrup vs Susan Blackmore — Consciousness and illusion (2023)
candidate.label: Idealism and conscious illusion
candidate.motion: Does analytic idealism adequately explain consciousness?
candidate.sourceNote: Public English captions cover the complete substantive conversation published by Curt Jaimungal in 2023. Selected speaker transitions and uncertain passages were checked against the recording. The duplicated opening preview, promotional material and moderator logistics receive no separate credit; no later substantive discussion is omitted. One unidentified, nonmaterial repeated boundary question is excluded from quotation and credit. Short quotations retain verified source wording; argument cards are faithful condensations. Blackmore rejects materialism and offers a limited critical method, not a completed rival metaphysics.
candidate.scoringNote: These AI-generated scores estimate argumentative performance in this transcript, not the truth of a worldview. They were computed exactly once from a frozen 33-move ledger after two isolated primary judgments and anonymous adjudication. Publication prose and subsequent fallacy and cognitive-bias review cannot alter the numerical result.
candidate.summary: Blackmore’s disciplined challenges expose gaps in Kastrup’s elegant idealist account, especially around boundaries and evidence, while her limited method avoids claiming a rival metaphysics.

pro.text: It takes away an extra ontic category
pro.context: Kastrup presents ontological economy as idealism’s principal gain: nature and perception remain mental, avoiding a transition from nonexperience to experience.

con.text: perhaps it's unfair to ask the idealist
con.context: Blackmore qualifies her regularity objection after recognizing that physics also reaches unexplained constants, limiting rather than abandoning her comparative challenge.

pro.words: Kastrup argues that illusionism either leaves phenomenal seeming intact, preserving the hard problem, or reduces experience to neuronal digests that generate an explanatory regress.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup presents a memorable dilemma: an experienced illusion already supplies phenomenality, while treating experience as a neuronal digest invites another question about why that digest appears experiential. Principal limitation: His attack largely targets eliminative formulations associated with Frankish and Dennett, whereas Blackmore immediately preserves experience and defines her own approach more modestly, making the reply less responsive to her actual position. Live burden: He must show that Blackmore's diagnostic account inherits the regress, or explain why a deliberately limited method cannot expose conceptual mistakes without becoming a rival metaphysical theory. Locked score: The move earns 72 because its logic is intelligible and clearly expressed, yet its warrant and charity weaken when a forceful objection to stronger illusionism is applied too broadly.

tags.label: Red herring
tags.context: He redirects Blackmore’s experience-preserving method toward eliminative theories she expressly rejects.

con.words: Blackmore treats the hard problem as a misleading dualist framing and redirects inquiry toward explaining how mistaken ideas about consciousness and self arise.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore establishes a clear methodological destination by asking how our conception of consciousness became misleading, rather than assuming that experience must somehow arise from brain activity. Principal limitation: The opening remains programmatic, offering little evidence or detailed mechanism for how the alleged conceptual illusions are produced, sustained, or experimentally distinguished from accurate introspection. Live burden: She needs to identify specific mistaken commitments and demonstrate that investigating their formation yields explanatory progress beyond renaming the hard problem as a meta-problem. Locked score: The move earns 81 because it directly defines her central burden, responds well to the inherited mind-body framing, and remains reasonably cautious, though its evidential support and constructive detail are still incomplete.

pro.words: Kastrup requests a definite illusionist hypothesis, arguing that broad diagnosis lacks content while eliminative accounts still cannot explain nonphenomenal representation of phenomenal states.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup correctly distinguishes a request for a testable, definite claim from an unfair demand that Blackmore produce a complete metaphysics, then identifies the representation gap in stronger eliminative accounts. Principal limitation: He relies on contentious portrayals of Frankish and Graziano and repeatedly treats those positions as representative, despite Blackmore's explicit refusal to deny phenomenal properties and her more restricted methodological purpose. Live burden: He must connect the alleged incoherence of mainstream eliminativism to Blackmore's actual thesis, rather than letting terminological frustration substitute for engagement with her diagnostic target. Locked score: The move earns 76 because it is relevant, structured, and substantially responsive, but its sweeping rhetoric and limited charity prevent the specificity challenge from decisively defeating her stated view.

tags.label: Red herring
tags.context: After Blackmore preserves phenomenal states, Kastrup continues attacking Frankish and Graziano’s eliminative positions.

con.words: Blackmore preserves subjective experience and defines illusionism as a modest diagnostic approach that rejects the hard problem's framing rather than competing to solve it.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore directly answers the dilemma by separating her position from phenomenal-state denial and limiting its aim to uncovering mistaken ideas about consciousness, self, and free will. Principal limitation: Her appeal to representation remains suggestive rather than explanatory, and saying the method is intentionally nonspecific risks protecting it from the ordinary standards used to compare theories or research programs. Live burden: She must show that this limited approach produces identifiable insights or tests, while maintaining the distinction between experience itself and inaccurate metacognitive interpretation. Locked score: The move earns 82 because it accurately narrows her burden, engages Kastrup's objection with notable charity, and preserves phenomenality, although the method's positive warrant and operational precision remain less developed than its defensive clarification.

con.words: Blackmore rejects materialism and any duty to supply a finished ontology, maintaining that exposing category mistakes can advance inquiry even before an alternative theory is complete.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore plainly disavows materialism, preserves experience, and explains why a critical method may legitimately diagnose the conscious-versus-unconscious process distinction without offering a finished metaphysical replacement. Principal limitation: Her proposed category mistake is asserted more than demonstrated, and the discussion of neural correlates does not yet show how researchers should reformulate experiments or what discoveries the method uniquely enables. Live burden: She must support the claim that these distinctions are genuinely confused and show how removing them creates progress rather than merely postponing a positive account. Locked score: The move earns 83 because it sharply corrects a false burden, answers Kastrup's demand without evasion, and calibrates its ambition unusually well, while its evidence and constructive consequences remain moderately underdeveloped.

pro.words: Kastrup accepts first-person inquiry alongside objective methods, then argues that affirming experience while rejecting dualism and eliminativism commits Blackmore to an idealist ontology.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup builds from genuine common ground, affirming introspection without dismissing neuroimaging or clinical evidence, and turns Blackmore's anti-materialist commitments into a concise conditional argument. Principal limitation: The conclusion does not follow exhaustively, because rejecting dualism and phenomenal elimination leaves multiple neutral-monist, panpsychist, process-based, or otherwise nonmaterialist possibilities besides Kastrup's idealism. Live burden: He must defend the excluded middle that places all experience-affirming monism within his mental category, and address rival accounts without treating a semantic classification as an ontological demonstration. Locked score: The move earns 70 because it is clear, relevant, and responsive to shared premises, but its central inference overreaches the available alternatives and is insufficiently charitable to Blackmore's deliberate agnosticism.

con.words: Blackmore rejects phenomenal-property denial while cautiously combining attention-schema theory, scientific research, and altered-state observation as complementary methods for investigating consciousness.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore gives her broad methodology concrete content by distinguishing her view from Frankish, presenting attention-schema theory as promising but incomplete, and integrating first-person practice with scientific and philosophical inquiry. Principal limitation: She does not establish that attention schemas explain experience rather than attention or report, and her personal explorations cannot independently validate the proposed model or adjudicate among competing ontologies. Live burden: She must specify which observable findings would count for or against the schema-based diagnosis and how altered-state evidence avoids being filtered through the very metacognitive errors under examination. Locked score: The move earns 79 because it is open, well calibrated, and constructively relevant, yet its empirical warrant and theoretical precision remain exploratory rather than decisive.

pro.words: Kastrup uses field theory against bounded-particle panpsychism and proposes one objective, nonlocalized field of subjectivity whose mental activity appears as the external world.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup offers a substantial positive ontology, explaining particles as field excitations and using a single field of subjectivity to avoid the combination problem while preserving an objective world. Principal limitation: Physics models nonlocalized fields without identifying them as experiential, and his claim that panpsychism assumes self-existing particles overlooks the alternative variants Blackmore expressly raises, making the metaphysical conclusion outrun the scientific premises. Live burden: He must justify the transition from unified physical modeling to one subjectivity and compare that interpretation with field-based panpsychism or other nonlocal ontologies. Locked score: The move earns 75 because it is ambitious, relevant, and supported by useful physical examples, but its central bridge is underargued and its treatment of rival positions is insufficiently calibrated.

con.words: Blackmore challenges Kastrup's forced choice by identifying panpsychism as another experience-affirming possibility and asking him to defend idealism's alleged uniqueness.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore targets the exact inferential weakness in Kastrup's claim that her commitments leave nowhere but idealism, supplying a direct counterexample and inviting a comparative defense rather than asserting her own dogma. Principal limitation: The challenge names a family of views without developing a specific version, evidential basis, or solution to familiar combination and individuation problems, so its constructive warrant remains deliberately thin in this metaphysical comparison. Live burden: She needs only to preserve a credible alternative to defeat exhaustiveness, but further detail would clarify whether the alternative truly differs from Kastrup's category or merely changes terminology. Locked score: The move earns 84 because it is exceptionally responsive, precise, and charitable as a diagnostic question, though its evidential development is limited by its brief scope.

pro.words: Kastrup argues that mentality can behave regularly and that perception compresses an objective mental world into a survival-relevant, entropy-limited physical dashboard.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup separates two questions and offers an intelligible account of perception: lawful mentality is possible, while organisms need selective representations because exhaustive mirroring would overwhelm useful action and internal stability. Principal limitation: The evolutionary dashboard mechanism is compatible with several ontologies, and the entropy claim is cited without enough explanation to show why the represented world must itself be mental rather than merely informationally compressed. Live burden: He must distinguish the empirical compression story from its idealist interpretation and explain regularity beyond asserting that nature behaves as it does. Locked score: The move earns 78 because it supplies a coherent, vivid, and burden-relevant model, but its warrant is compressed and its most developed mechanism does not uniquely support analytic idealism.

con.words: Blackmore asks what idealism adds by calling objective fields mental when their stable laws and regular behavior still require explanation.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore isolates the motion's comparative standard by asking whether changing the ontological label explains the world's regularities or simply inherits them, directly challenging the claimed adequacy of idealism. Principal limitation: Her suggestion that materialism has answers is underdeveloped and later qualified, since physical theories also describe stable patterns without explaining why ultimate constants or laws possess their particular values or obtain at all. Live burden: She must distinguish demands that any metaphysics faces from explanatory transitions peculiar to Kastrup's view, while recognizing that avoiding dualism may itself count as a genuine theoretical gain. Locked score: The move earns 86 because it is sharply responsive, highly relevant, and clearly framed, with only a bounded weakness in its initial, insufficiently defended comparison to materialism.

pro.words: Kastrup says idealism removes an unnecessary nonmental category, allowing external qualities and perceptual qualities to interact without an ontological transition.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup finally states a distinct comparative benefit: if external and internal states are both qualitative mentality, their causal relation requires no emergence of experience from something defined as nonexperiential. Principal limitation: The familiar interaction among thoughts, emotions, and fantasies does not establish that external nature is a mental subject, and shared category membership alone does not explain the detailed laws governing cross-boundary modulation. Live burden: He must warrant the external mentality premise and show that ontological economy delivers explanatory constraints rather than merely redescribing every causal process in mental terms without new predictions. Locked score: The move earns 84 because it directly answers Blackmore, clearly advances the motion, and presents a coherent advantage, while the analogy and evidence remain incomplete.

con.words: Blackmore observes that selective, evolution-shaped perception fits materialist and other accounts too, so the dashboard mechanism alone provides no distinctive evidence for idealism.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore identifies the decisive underdetermination: attention, evolutionary relevance, and perceptual compression can all be accepted without treating the external world as mental, so the dashboard story cannot independently select idealism. Principal limitation: She does not fully engage Kastrup's separate economy claim that idealism removes the mind-from-nonmind transition, and her references to materialism sit awkwardly beside her explicit rejection of that metaphysics. Live burden: She should distinguish borrowing an ontology-neutral mechanism for criticism from endorsing materialism, then test whether Kastrup's ontic reduction adds any novel prediction or explanation. Locked score: The move earns 89 because it is exceptionally clear, responsive, and burden-focused, with strong warrant and charity despite leaving the ontological-economy reply for the next exchange.

pro.words: Kastrup treats matter, brains included, as the observable appearance of dissociated mental activity, making neural and experiential changes two perspectives on one process.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup gives a direct idealist account of neural correlation: brains are not producers of experience but outward representations of the same dissociated activity known inwardly as experience. Principal limitation: The formulation predicts correlation at a broad level but does not derive specific neural relationships, establish that dissociative boundaries exist cosmically, or independently support the identity between material appearance and mentality. Live burden: He must provide a noncircular criterion for boundaries and explain how the one-process view constrains which neural changes accompany which experiences better than rival interpretations of the same findings. Locked score: The move earns 81 because it is coherent, responsive, and central to his burden, while its empirical warrant and mechanism remain less developed than its elegant redescription.

con.words: Blackmore presses idealism to explain structured relationships among neural firing, hormones, bodily feeling, thought, and emotion rather than merely classifying everything as mental.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore converts an abstract relabeling concern into a concrete explanatory demand, emphasizing that neurotransmitters, hormones, neural activity, and felt states display structured temporal correlations any adequate account must preserve. Principal limitation: The move is primarily a challenge and does not specify which observed correlations would discriminate idealism from competing accounts, while some production language risks assuming the causal direction still at issue. Live burden: She must show that Kastrup's intrinsic-extrinsic identity leaves empirical relationships unexplained, rather than merely redescribing them, and identify what additional account adequacy requires. Locked score: The move earns 88 because it is precise, empirically grounded, highly responsive, and fair to the acknowledged correlations, despite remaining diagnostic rather than fully constructive.

pro.words: Kastrup defines dissociation as inferential isolation and cites state-dependent blindness plus ordinary forgetting to show that mentality can divide into mutually inaccessible perspectives.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup supplies both a conceptual definition and a concrete clinical illustration, linking inferential isolation to measurable, state-dependent loss of visual-cortex activity and to softer everyday failures of cognitive access. Principal limitation: A psychiatric division within one human organism shows that informational partition can occur, but does not establish that universal mentality exists or divides into private subjects by the same mechanism outside nervous systems. Live burden: He must explain how inferential isolation scales beyond brains, identify its necessary and sufficient conditions, and connect the reported study to the metaphysical individuation claim without analogy alone. Locked score: The move earns 82 because it is clear, responsive, and unusually well grounded for his dissociation case, although the cosmic extrapolation remains unresolved.

con.words: Blackmore requests the simplest clear account of a dissociative boundary, noting that Kastrup invokes partitions within organisms, between persons, and across the world.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore asks the indispensable mechanism question in clearly attributed language: what common criterion individuates the boundaries doing explanatory work within a person, between people, and between a person and the wider world. Principal limitation: The move does not propose an alternative account or operational test, but as a focused challenge it need not shoulder a positive metaphysical burden that Blackmore has expressly and consistently declined. Live burden: She must assess Kastrup's forthcoming inferential-isolation answer fairly and show whether it actually identifies boundaries rather than merely naming restricted access without an independently observable boundary condition. Locked score: The move earns 87 because it is precise, responsive, charitable, and central to testing dissociation, with evidential development appropriately limited by its interrogative role.

pro.words: Kastrup proposes life and metabolism as the outward appearance of dissociation, with neural correlates displaying the mental activity enclosed by each living boundary.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup answers the location question directly by identifying biology as the extrinsic appearance of nature's dissociative process and neural correlates as the visible signature of activity within that boundary. Principal limitation: Imaging that distinguishes genuine dissociation from acting establishes an organism-level signature, not the further identity between all life and partitions of a universal subject; the extrapolation therefore remains largely asserted. Live burden: He must justify why metabolism is sufficient for subject individuation, address borderline biological cases, and derive the proposed intrinsic-extrinsic relation independently of idealism. Locked score: Its 76 reflects a direct, intelligible answer about biological location, offset by sparse support for the universal generalization and a serious risk of assuming the very metaphysics at issue.

con.words: Blackmore accepts clinical dissociation but argues that brain-level cases do not establish organism-world boundaries or divisions within a universal field of mentality.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore grants the local evidence and then precisely isolates the missing bridge: a dissociative identity case inside one nervous system does not by itself reveal boundaries throughout an allegedly mental cosmos. Principal limitation: She does not explore whether Kastrup's framework requires identical mechanisms at both scales or merely an analogous pattern of restricted inference, leaving some room for a more modest functional response. Live burden: She should test the proposed biological marker and ask what observations could distinguish genuine world-scale dissociation from ordinary organismic separation under rival ontologies. Locked score: The move earns 92 because it combines exceptional responsiveness, clarity, calibration, and burden relevance, while grounding its criticism in a careful concession rather than denying the clinical phenomenon.

pro.words: Kastrup distinguishes experience from explicit awareness and report, arguing that inattentional blindness may remove metaconscious access without showing that phenomenal experience disappeared.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup draws a useful distinction between phenomenal occurrence and explicit knowledge of occurrence, using breathing, attention, and report to challenge inferences from unresponsiveness to absence of experience. Principal limitation: Preserved neural processing or later reports do not establish continuous phenomenality, and asserting that strictly unconscious states never occur extends far beyond the examples and ordinary attention cases supplied. Live burden: He must provide evidence that unattended processing is experienced rather than merely available for action, and clarify how his distinction supports idealism instead of a broadly compatible theory of consciousness. Locked score: The move earns 75 because it is clear and responsive with a valuable conceptual core, but its universal conclusion is weakly warranted and insufficiently calibrated.

con.words: Blackmore uses inattentional blindness and visual shortcuts to show that access, processing, and report can separate through ordinary cognition without favoring idealism.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore offers familiar, concrete demonstrations in which people miss visible stimuli or report repeated content they did not inspect, illustrating how perception and later report depend on selective processing. Principal limitation: These ordinary effects differ from the clinical state-dependent blindness Kastrup cites and do not directly answer his claim that dissociation can create robust inferential isolation within a larger mentality. Live burden: She must show that cognitive explanations cover the relevant clinical evidence and that dissociation-like phenomena remain ontologically neutral even when their neural signatures change markedly. Locked score: The move earns 82 because its evidence, clarity, and calibration are strong, while its responsiveness and motion-level consequence are more limited than those of her direct cosmic-scope objection.

pro.words: Kastrup argues that calling any mismatch between appearance and reality an illusion makes illusionism too broad to distinguish a substantive consciousness thesis.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup states a clean semantic test: because scientific inquiry routinely corrects appearances, a label covering every such correction contributes little discriminating content to a theory of consciousness. Principal limitation: Blackmore had just narrowed her target to metacognitive ownership and self-narration, so this reply addresses her earlier generic wording more than the strongest live version of her position in the exchange. Live burden: He must explain why her specific claims about constructed ownership remain trivial or incoherent, rather than showing only that an unrestricted dictionary definition would be unhelpful for distinguishing competing accounts. Locked score: The move earns 75 because its conditional logic, illustration, and clarity are strong, but reduced responsiveness and charity materially limit its relevance to the newly specified account.

tags.label: Red herring
tags.context: Kastrup attacks illusionism as broadly covering nearly every scientific correction after Blackmore narrows its target.

con.words: Blackmore locates illusion in metacognitive stories of a self owning experience, citing meditation in which experience continues without an owner, time, or spatial framing.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore turns a broad method into a specific target: reflective stories of an owner can disappear while experience continues, supporting a distinction between underlying occurrence and constructed metacognitive interpretation. Principal limitation: Her meditation report is personal and interpretively loaded, so it cannot by itself establish that ownership, time, and space are always false rather than temporarily absent or differently represented during unusual attention states. Live burden: She must connect this phenomenology to publicly testable evidence and clarify which metacognitive claims are erroneous without denying the practical organization supplied by self-models. Locked score: The move earns 86 because it is highly responsive, precise, charitable, and central to her burden, though its evidential base and underlying ontology remain deliberately limited.

pro.words: Kastrup agrees that selfhood and dualist categories can mislead, then recasts needles, wine, and other apparent physical causes as representations of mental interactions.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup acknowledges genuine convergence with Blackmore and applies his ontology to concrete causal examples, explaining apparent physical-to-mental influence as mental activity crossing a dissociative boundary. Principal limitation: The reinterpretation is coherent within idealism but largely presupposes that all material objects represent mentality, so it does not independently establish the ontology or explain detailed causal regularities. Live burden: He must show that the account yields constraints, predictions, or comparative explanations beyond translating physical descriptions into mental terms, while retaining Blackmore's narrower diagnosis of reification. Locked score: The move earns 80 because it is clear, relevant, and substantially responsive, with good calibration in acknowledging agreement, yet its evidence and explanatory leverage remain incomplete.

con.words: Blackmore specifies that illusionism targets reifying consciousness as a separable entity produced by brains, not the broader claim that every physical appearance is illusory.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore answers the overbreadth objection with her clearest boundary: the target is metalevel talk that turns consciousness into a separate thing and then asks how brains produce it. Principal limitation: She still offers limited evidence that this conceptual diagnosis explains the relevant data, and her language shifts among everyday concepts, scientific theories, and introspective constructions without fully separating those levels of analysis. Live burden: She must identify which claims are dispensable reifications, show how removing them changes research practice, and avoid treating every production model as dualistic by definition or linguistic habit. Locked score: The move earns 87 because it directly resolves the live semantic challenge with precision, relevance, and unusual charity, though the method's positive empirical payoff remains less developed than its diagnostic force.

pro.words: Kastrup treats laws as primitive properties of nature and the personal ego as a useful metacognitive narrative layered upon an organism's body schema.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup accepts an ultimate explanatory stopping point shared by metaphysical rivals and offers a functional reason for self-representation, distinguishing basic experience, body schema, and reflective metacognition. Principal limitation: The fork-to-mouth example initially overstates the ego's necessity, as Blackmore's animal objection shows, and saying nature behaves according to its properties explains little about why idealism should posit those properties. Live burden: He must clarify which coordination functions require metacognitive selfhood rather than body schema alone and how the layered model follows from analytic idealism specifically, not merely cognitive organization. Locked score: The move earns 76 because it is coherent, responsive, and reasonably calibrated after clarification, but its evidence and distinct explanatory contribution remain modest.

con.words: Blackmore concedes that physics also cannot explain why fundamental constants have their values, so ultimate regularity cannot fairly be demanded from idealism alone.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore openly limits her strongest recurring objection, recognizing that explanations in any framework may terminate at brute constants or laws and refusing to impose an asymmetric burden on idealism. Principal limitation: The concession concerns ultimate values, not intermediate questions about whether Kastrup's model explains structured correlations, perceptual representation, or the emergence of biological boundaries, so its scope must remain carefully narrow. Live burden: She should preserve those local explanatory challenges while granting that no rival supplies an endless chain of deeper reasons for every regularity. Locked score: The move earns 89 because its logic, responsiveness, clarity, and especially calibration are excellent, with strong comparative relevance and only the ordinary evidential limits inherent in a philosophical concession.

pro.words: Kastrup argues that imperfect dissociation could allow tiny, emotionally conditioned information leakage while leaving laboratory controls and ordinary scientific results largely intact.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup anticipates an apparent conflict with scientific practice by limiting any proposed porosity to weak, context-sensitive effects, preserving the everyday privacy of minds and most experimental controls. Principal limitation: He offers no independent evidence that emotional circumstances weaken dissociation, and explaining laboratory non-detection through stronger laboratory boundaries risks insulating the claim from the controlled tests needed to establish it. Live burden: He must state conditions that make leakage predictably detectable and distinguish his account from coincidence, selective recall, or other ordinary explanations. Locked score: The move earns 69 because it is intelligible and responsive as a compatibility argument, but its empirical warrant, calibration, and falsifiability remain substantially weaker than its metaphysical possibility claim.

tags.label: Special pleading
tags.context: Kastrup says telepathic leakage occurs in emotional life but disappears under controlled laboratory conditions.

con.words: Blackmore would revise her understanding of mind if adequately designed, sufficiently powered, statistically sound experiments produced convincing evidence of telepathy.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore states a concrete revision standard and explains its consequence: reliable telepathy would undermine informational independence assumed in psychological controls and alter interpretation across placebo and related research. Principal limitation: Her initial suggestion that most science would be wrong is broader than the specific methodological disruption she later describes, and she does not define an effect size, replication threshold, or acceptable protocol. Live burden: She must apply the same openness to credible contemporary evidence while distinguishing serious anomalies from results produced by weak design, multiplicity, or leakage. Locked score: The move earns 85 because it is clear, falsifiable, responsive, and methodologically grounded, with only bounded overstatement and incomplete operational detail preventing an even stronger result.

pro.words: Kastrup recounts his girlfriend's detailed dream about her grandmother and the confirming callback as a personally compelling but uncontrolled case of possible information leakage.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup supplies a concrete chronology with multiple matching details: his girlfriend described her grandmother bandaged beside two daughters, then a callback revealed a recent stroke and reassuring medical status. Principal limitation: The report is retrospective, secondhand in crucial parts, and uncontrolled, leaving coincidence, memory reconstruction, unnoticed cues, and selective emphasis unevaluated; it therefore establishes no independently verified paranormal event. Live burden: He must document timing and prior statements, compare alternative explanations, and show that such cases occur above an appropriate base rate before treating them as evidence for porous dissociation. Locked score: The move earns 61 because its narrative is specific and clear, but evidential warrant, responsiveness to controlled-evidence demands, and calibration are weak.

tags.label: Base-rate neglect
tags.context: Kastrup treats one vivid dream match as compelling without comparing ordinary dream and coincidence frequencies.

tags.label: Subjective validation
tags.context: Kastrup says a personally witnessed dream coincidence was so specific he could not dismiss it.

con.words: Blackmore welcomes testable telepathy but argues that parapsychology has not produced convincing evidence and viable theory sufficient for controlled comparison of mechanisms.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore distinguishes excitement about a possible phenomenon from belief that it has been established, and connects credible evidence to the next scientific step of testing competing mechanisms. Principal limitation: Her broad historical conclusion is asserted without reviewing particular studies in this exchange, and her later admission of limited familiarity with research after about 2000 restricts how confidently it applies to current literature. Live burden: She must assess representative contemporary evidence under her announced design and statistical standards, rather than relying solely on the field's past failure to mature into cumulative science. Locked score: The move earns 86 because it directly answers Kastrup's compatibility claim with disciplined evidential standards and strong calibration, despite compressed documentation and dated coverage.

pro.words: Kastrup calls materialism explanatorily deficient, internally contradictory, and empirically inadequate, declining an ordinary revision condition while contrasting a concrete hypothetical multiverse test.
pro.critique: Strongest feature: Kastrup consolidates three distinct objections and usefully contrasts his refusal with a specific kind of anomalous energy result that could increase his confidence in a multiverse. Principal limitation: The answer largely evades the requested revision condition, caricatures materialism through the Flying Spaghetti Monster comparison, and presents contested interpretations of quantum experiments and intellectual history with excessive certainty. Live burden: He must formulate the strongest coherent materialist alternative, identify evidence that would discriminate it from idealism, and defend rather than assume his empirical and historical claims. Locked score: The move earns 57 because it contains a recognizable comparative argument, but weak warrant, poor responsiveness, and severely disproportionate calibration overwhelm its clarity and relevance.

tags.label: Confirmation bias
tags.context: Kastrup says changing his view would require becoming a child and unlearning forty-eight years.

tags.label: Red herring
tags.context: Asked for a revision condition, Kastrup shifts to the Flying Spaghetti Monster, church politics, and Enlightenment history.

con.words: Blackmore declines an instant case judgment, explaining that fair parapsychology review is laborious and that her deep literature familiarity ended around the turn of the century.
con.critique: Strongest feature: Blackmore resists giving a glib explanation of Kastrup's anecdote, separates the host's researcher prompts from her own commitments, and candidly dates the limits of her expertise. Principal limitation: She does not answer the particular case or substantiate her reference to problematic practices, so the reply offers disciplined scope control rather than a substantive rebuttal of the alleged coincidence and its evidential force. Live burden: She must examine the documentation and relevant current literature before drawing a case-specific or field-wide conclusion, while no concession follows merely from declining hurried analysis of an unfamiliar retrospective report. Locked score: The move earns 80 because its charity, caution, and clarity are strong, but its responsiveness and evidence are necessarily bounded by the explicit refusal to adjudicate immediately.

strengths: Kastrup offers a coherent one-category ontology that directly addresses the hard problem by refusing any fundamental transition from nonexperience to experience.
His dashboard account separates external reality from perception while explaining selective representation through biological usefulness and manageable informational demands.
The dissociation proposal combines a clear inferential-isolation concept with clinical evidence, giving private minds a more concrete mechanism than simple assertion.

blunders.text: Kastrup repeatedly moves from compatible observations to specifically idealist conclusions without showing why rival ontologies cannot explain the same patterns.
His closing materialism answer supplies no usable revision condition and treats a contested dream coincidence as suggestive despite lacking controlled verification.

strengths: Blackmore consistently identifies the missing comparative bridge: calling nature mental must explain regularity, representation, neural correlation, and individual boundaries better.
She narrows illusionism to a critical method about ownership and reification, avoiding both denial of experience and an unnecessary complete rival metaphysics.
Her strongest replies combine precise questions with fair concessions, especially granting brute regularities and declining to adjudicate unfamiliar parapsychology evidence hastily.

blunders.text: Her early materialist comparisons overstate what physical theory explains, a weakness she later acknowledges when conceding that ultimate constants remain brute.
Her meditation-based account of ownerless experience remains personally reported and underconnected to public evidence, limiting its reach beyond methodological suggestion.

finalArgument.thesis: Analytic idealism best explains consciousness by treating experience as fundamental, physical appearances as representations, and private minds as informationally isolated regions within one field of subjectivity.
premises: Experience is immediately given in ordinary awareness, whereas a wholly nonexperiential substrate is theoretical and leaves the emergence of qualitative awareness conceptually unexplained.
Treating external nature and perception as different kinds of mental state permits causal interaction without crossing an ontological divide between matter and lived experience.

Perception need not reproduce reality itself, because evolved organisms benefit from compressed dashboards that preserve action-relevant structure while hiding overwhelming underlying environmental detail.

Clinical and ordinary dissociations show that one experiential system can contain informationally isolated processes, making divided subjectivity at least conceptually coherent and empirically motivated.

Neural correlations can be interpreted as the external appearance of dissociated mental activity, preserving established scientific findings without identifying brains as the literal producers of experience.
finalArgument.conclusion: A single experiential ontology therefore unifies consciousness, perception, and neural correlation more economically than materialism, provided dissociative boundaries can be independently characterized and tested.

newArguments.title: Comparative Prediction Ledger
newArguments.text: Idealism gains explanatory force only when its reinterpretation of evidence constrains expectations differently from rivals. Kastrup could specify a ledger of cases in which identity between mental activity and physical appearance predicts correlations, dissociative failures, or perceptual distortions that a production model would not independently expect. A critic may object that mature neuroscience could absorb every listed pattern without changing ontology. That objection makes comparative risk essential: the ledger must include outcomes that would count against idealism, not merely phenomena it can redescribe afterward. Even one well-defined divergent prediction would convert ontological economy from an aesthetic advantage into an empirically discriminating research claim.

newArguments.title: Boundary Hierarchy Test
newArguments.text: Dissociation becomes more credible as a cosmic mechanism if boundaries form a nested hierarchy governed by one observable principle. Kastrup could predict that stronger inferential isolation tracks more stable biological integration, while partial boundary failures produce graded, reproducible information exchange rather than all-or-nothing privacy. The obvious objection is that this pattern may simply restate familiar neural connectivity without supporting universal consciousness. To answer, the account must identify a measure derived from idealism that applies across clinical divisions, ordinary organisms, and any alleged anomalous leakage. Failure of that measure would weaken the metaphysics; success would connect local evidence to the disputed world-scale extrapolation.

newArguments.title: Economy With Exclusions
newArguments.text: Removing a nonmental ontic category is valuable only if the resulting theory also excludes incoherent or unsupported possibilities. Kastrup could strengthen his economy argument by deriving limits on which experiential structures can appear as stable physical worlds, rather than allowing any regularity as a primitive disposition of mind. Blackmore can fairly object that every metaphysics eventually reaches brute facts, but that concession does not erase intermediate explanatory duties. If idealism identifies structural constraints linking qualitative relations, perceptual dashboards, and lawful public measurements, it offers more than relabeling. Without such exclusions, simplicity remains genuine but shallow; with them, economy could yield a disciplined explanatory program.

finalArgument.thesis: Analytic idealism remains underjustified because its central observations fit multiple ontologies, while dissociation, representation, and mental causation are described without sufficiently discriminating mechanisms or evidence.
premises: Illusionism can target mistaken metacognitive stories about ownership, temporal unity, and reification without denying experience or committing its critic to a materialist ontology.
Perceptual dashboards explain why appearances differ from reality, but that functional account remains compatible with materialist, panpsychist, and idealist interpretations of the underlying world.
Clinical dissociation establishes informational division inside particular nervous systems, not the existence or partition of a universal subject extending beyond all biological organization.
Calling neural activity the outward appearance of experience preserves observed correlation, yet does not derive specific pairings or outperform rival causal interpretations of neurological evidence.

Personal coincidence reports may motivate serious inquiry, but rational revision should depend on documented, controlled, replicated evidence assessed against ordinary alternative explanations and relevant base rates.
finalArgument.conclusion: The critical verdict should therefore remain provisional but unfavorable: idealism is coherent and economical, yet it has not earned adequacy through distinctive explanations, boundary criteria, or controlled support.

newArguments.title: Asymmetric Detail Challenge
newArguments.text: A successful metaphysics need not explain why every ultimate law holds, but it should explain why some intermediate structures follow from its commitments. Blackmore could separate brute constants from derivable architecture and ask idealism to predict features of perceptual compression, neural correlation, or biological individuation. Kastrup may answer that physical theories also begin from unexplained structures. That reply is fair only at the same explanatory level: shared ignorance about constants does not excuse missing links between universal mentality and particular organisms. The consequence is a sharper burden that respects Blackmore’s concession while preserving her central criticism of explanatory relabeling.

newArguments.title: Ownership Intervention Program
newArguments.text: Blackmore’s claim about constructed ownership can move beyond meditation reports through interventions that alter metacognition while preserving task-relevant experience. Studies could compare confidence, temporal self-location, agency reports, and perceptual discrimination before and after targeted attention training or neural disruption. A result showing altered ownership alongside stable discrimination would support her distinction, though it would not prove that ownership is always illusory or settle ontology. Null results, or changes confined to verbal report, would narrow the thesis. This program converts a philosophical method into public evidence while respecting the limited claim that some reflective interpretations, not experience itself, are mistaken.

newArguments.title: Anecdote-to-Evidence Protocol
newArguments.text: Reports like Kastrup’s girlfriend’s dream deserve neither dismissal nor immediate metaphysical weight. Blackmore could propose prospective timestamping, preregistered matching criteria, blinded judges, comparison pools, and replication across emotionally salient relationships. Critics may worry that laboratory structure suppresses the very conditions under which weak effects occur. The protocol can therefore include naturalistic prospective collection while preserving advance records and explicit base rates. If matches remain exceptional under those safeguards, competing mechanisms become worth testing; if they do not, memory and coincidence retain priority. This approach makes openness and skepticism operational rather than treating either a vivid narrative or field history as decisive.
